title: A. & T. Sabatini v. PA PUC - 237 C.D. 2025

documents.text:
IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA

Andrew and Theresa Sabatini,                  :
                      Petitioners             :
                                              :
              v.                              :
                                              :
Pennsylvania Public Utility                   :
Commission,                                   :   No. 237 C.D. 2025
                         Respondent           :   Submitted: May 14, 2026


BEFORE:       HONORABLE ANNE E. COVEY, Judge
              HONORABLE STELLA M. TSAI, Judge
              HONORABLE MARY HANNAH LEAVITT, Senior Judge


OPINION NOT REPORTED

MEMORANDUM OPINION
BY JUDGE TSAI                                              FILED: October 14, 2026
       Petitioners Andrew Sabatini and Theresa Sabatini petition, pro se, for review
of an order of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC or Commission),
which affirmed the decision of an administrative law judge (ALJ) and dismissed
Petitioners’ complaint with prejudice. We affirm.
                                   I. BACKGROUND
       This Court recently explained:
       On November 14, 2008, the General Assembly enacted Act 129, [1]
       which required [electrical distribution companies (EDCs)] with more
       than 100,000 customers . . . to file smart meter technology [2]
       procurement and installation plans [(Procurement and Installation

       1
         Act of October 15, 2008, P.L. 1592. Act 129 amended the Public Utility Code (Code),
which is set forth in its entirety at 66 Pa. C.S. §§ 101-3316.
       2
          “Smart meters, also known as advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) meters, record
electricity consumption on at least an hourly basis using radio frequency (RF) electromagnetic
energy.” Hughes v. Pa. Pub. Util. Comm’n, 322 A.3d 982, 987 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2024).
        Plans)] with the Commission within nine months. On June 24, 2009,
       the Commission issued its Smart Meter Implementation Order, which
       set forth requirements for the smart meter plans and procedures for the
       submission, review, and approval thereof.

Kline v. Pa. Pub. Util. Comm’n, 352 A.3d 1086, 1090 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2026) (footnotes
added).
       We summarize the relevant findings of fact of ALJ Emily DeVoe, as follows.
Petitioners reside in Acme, Pennsylvania. Certified Record (C.R.) at 842a. West
Penn Power Company (West Penn)3 is an EDC with at least 100,000 customers, and
West Penn provides residential electrical service to Petitioners at their residence. Id.
at 842a-843a. The Commission approved West Penn’s Procurement and Installation
Plan on June 30, 2011, and it approved West Penn’s smart meter deployment plan
on June 5, 2014. Id. at 843a. West Penn’s smart meter deployment plan does not
include any provision for its customers to opt-out from the installation of a smart
meter. Id.
       Petitioners filed a complaint with the Commission on October 9, 2018,
seeking to retain the analog electricity meter at their residence and to block the
installation of a smart meter. Id. at 919a. ALJ Jeffrey Watson held an evidentiary
hearing on February 20, 2020. Id. at 924a. On November 4, 2020, the Commission
entered an order which stayed the proceedings in this matter, along with others
involving similar claims. Id. at 739a-741a.
       The Commission lifted its stay order on November 14, 2023. Id. at 744a-
753a. The Commission entered an order on November 27, 2023, reassigning this
matter to ALJ DeVoe. Id. at 754a-755a. On December 5, 2023, ALJ DeVoe entered

       3
         On June 18, 2025, this Court granted West Penn’s application to intervene in this matter.
Further, we note that West Penn subsequently merged with several other companies and is now
known as FirstEnergy Pennsylvania Electric Company. C.R. at 917a n.3 (Commission’s Op. &
Order). However, we will refer to the EDC as “West Penn” throughout for consistency.


                                                2
 an order providing that the parties may, but were not required to, file briefs on or
before January 12, 2024. Id. at 768a. Petitioners filed a motion for extension of
time to file a brief on January 9, 2024, explaining that a family member had recently
passed away and Petitioners did not have enough time to review the transcript at the
Commission offices in Pittsburgh and to prepare their brief. Id. at 771a-772a. ALJ
DeVoe denied the motion on the following day. Id. at 774a-777a.
       ALJ DeVoe issued an initial decision on June 4, 2024, denying Petitioners’
complaint. Id. at 830a-849a. Petitioners filed timely exceptions to that initial
decision. Id. at 885a-882a. The Commission subsequently entered an opinion and
order dismissing Petitioners’ complaint with prejudice on December 19, 2024. Id.
at 915a-945a. Petitioners then petitioned this Court for review.
                                          II. ISSUES
       On appeal,4 Petitioners raise five issues, which we consolidate into three
issues: (1) whether the Commission erred by concluding that Section 2807(f) of the
Code, 66 Pa. C.S. § 2807(f), mandates universal installation of smart meters;
(2) whether mandatory smart meter installation violates Article I, Section 8 of the
Pennsylvania Constitution; and (3) whether ALJ DeVoe violated Petitioners’
procedural due process rights. Additionally, West Penn requests that we dismiss this
appeal as moot.5

       4
         “This Court’s review of a Commission adjudication determines whether constitutional
rights have been violated, an error of law has been committed, or the Commission’s findings and
conclusions are, or are not, supported by substantial evidence.” Schmukler v. Pa. Pub. Util.
Comm’n, 302 A.3d 247, 250 n.6 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2023) (citations, quotation marks, and brackets
omitted). Further, statutory interpretation is a pure question of law subject to de novo review. See
McCloskey v. Pa. Pub. Util. Comm’n, 255 A.3d 416, 423 n.13 (Pa. 2021).
       5
         Whether a case is moot presents a “pure question[] of law, and therefore this Court’s
standard of review is de novo and our scope of review is plenary.” Commonwealth v. Dixon, 907
A.2d 468, 472 (Pa. 2006).


                                                 3
                                   III. DISCUSSION
                                     A. Mootness
      Before we address the merits of Petitioners’ claims, we first address West
Penn’s request to dismiss this appeal as moot. West Penn argues that “Petitioners’
appeal is moot because it is impossible for the Court to grant their request for an
opt-out of the smart meter.” West Penn’s Brief at 18. Specifically, West Penn
contends that the Pennsylvania Supreme Court’s decision in Povacz v. Pennsylvania
Public Utility Commission, 280 A.3d 975 (Pa. 2022) (Povacz II), is controlling and
bars this Court from granting Petitioners the relief that they are seeking. Id. at 17-20.
      Petitioners respond that this appeal is not moot because there are unresolved
constitutional questions. Petitioners’ Am. Reply Brief at 29-31. Alternatively,
Petitioners contend that this case satisfies all three exceptions to the mootness
doctrine. Id. at 31-33.
      This Court has explained:
      It is well settled that an actual case or controversy must be extant at all
      stages of litigation, not merely at the time that a complaint is filed;
      otherwise, this Court will dismiss an appeal as moot. An “actual case
      or controversy” is one that is real rather than hypothetical and affects
      someone in a concrete manner so as to provide a factual predicate for
      reasoned adjudication. Exceptions to the mootness doctrine may be
      made where the conduct complained of is capable of repetition yet
      likely to evade judicial review, where the case involves issues of great
      public importance, or where one party will suffer a detriment without
      the court’s decision.

Gray v. Philadelphia Dist. Att’y’s Off., 311 A.3d 1230, 1236 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2024)
(citations and quotation marks omitted). “An issue can become moot during the
pendency of an appeal due to an intervening change in the facts of the case or due to
an intervening change in the applicable law. In that case, an opinion of this Court is




                                           4
 rendered advisory in nature.” Consumer Educ. & Prot. Ass’n v. Pub. Util. Comm’n,
847 A.2d 789, 794 n.9 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2004) (citation omitted).
      West Penn relies on our Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Povacz II, which
the Supreme Court issued after Petitioners’ complaint and before the Commission’s
decision and the instant appeal, in support of its argument that this appeal should be
dismissed as moot. West Penn essentially contends that because Povacz II, in West
Penn’s view, precludes this Court from granting Petitioners the relief that they seek,
the appeal is moot. Whether Povacz II controls the issue in this case is not relevant
to the question of mootness. Rather, the applicability of Povacz II is relevant to the
merits of this appeal. Put another way, this Court could conclude that Petitioners’
arguments lack merit in the face of Povacz II, but that does not mean that the appeal
is moot. Petitioners have not withdrawn their complaint in the light of the Supreme
Court’s decision in Povacz II, and, therefore, an actual case which affects Petitioners
in a concrete manner still exists. See Gray, 311 A.3d at 1236. For this reason, we
deny West Penn’s request to dismiss this appeal as moot, and we will address the
merits of this appeal.

  B. Whether Section 2807(f) of the Code Mandates Universal Installation of
                                Smart Meters
      Turning to the merits of this appeal, Petitioners’ first three claims relate to the
interpretation and application of Section 2807(f) of the Code. First, Petitioners argue
that Povacz II should no longer be considered controlling in light of the United States
Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369
(2024) (Loper Bright), which overruled Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources
Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984) (Chevron). Petitioners’ Am. Brief at 20-
33. Second, Petitioners argue that, for purposes of construing Section 2807(f) of the
Code, neither the plain language nor the legislative history of that section supports

                                           5
 the Commission’s interpretation that the General Assembly, when it enacted Section
2807(f), intended to require universal installation of smart meters for all customers
of an EDC. Id. at 34-63. Lastly, Petitioners argue that the Commission erred in
interpreting the term “depreciation schedule” in Section 2807(f)(2)(iii) to mean
“deployment schedule” as part of mandatory smart meter installation. Id. at 38-40,
42. As to the last two arguments, this Court will only reach them if we embrace
Petitioners’ argument that Povacz II is no longer controlling given the United States
Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright.
      According to Petitioners, Loper Bright “fundamentally transformed
administrative law and how courts review agency interpretations of statutes.” Id. at
20. Petitioners claim that, in Povacz II, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court implicitly
applied the doctrine of Chevron deference when interpreting Act 129 because the
Povacz II Court “gave weight to the [Commission’s] specialized knowledge of
utility regulation,” “emphasized that the [Commission] had interpreted Act 129 to
require mandatory installation since 2009,” “noted that [EDCs] relied on the
[Commission’s] interpretation when making investment decisions,” and “referenced
billions of dollars utilit[y companies] spent on smart meter infrastructure based on
the [Commission’s] mandate.” Id. at 24 (citing Povacz II, 280 A.3d at 987-88). For
those reasons, Petitioners argue that Loper Bright “requires this Court to use
traditional tools of statutory construction to independently determine Act 129’s
meaning.”    Id. at 28.   Petitioners additionally contend that this Court should
reimplement its holding from Povacz v. Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission,
241 A.3d 481 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2020) (en banc) (Povacz I), which concluded that
Section 2807(f) of the Code does not mandate smart meter installation. Id. at 31-33.




                                         6
       The Commission and West Penn respond that Loper Bright applies to federal
courts interpreting federal law, and it does not apply to Pennsylvania courts
interpreting Pennsylvania statutes. Commission’s Brief at 14-15; West Penn’s Brief
at 23. Further, the Commission and West Penn argue that Povacz II remains good
law and is controlling here. Commission’s Brief at 17-20; West Penn’s Brief at
20-24.
      As to the federal concept of Chevron deference,
      the term “Chevron deference” refers to the United States Supreme
      Court’s seminal decision in Chevron, U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources
      Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984), which stated that federal
      law had “long recognized that considerable weight should be accorded
      to an executive department’s construction of a statutory scheme it is
      entrusted to administer[.]” [Chevron], 467 U.S. at 844 (footnote
      omitted).

Marcellus Shale Coal. v. Dep’t of Env’t Prot., 292 A.3d 921, 928 (Pa. 2023).
      Under the Chevron doctrine, courts utilized
      a two-step framework to interpret statutes administered by federal
      agencies. After determining that a case satisfie[d] the various
      preconditions . . . for Chevron [deference] to apply, a reviewing court
      [would] first assess “whether Congress has directly spoken to the
      precise question at issue.” [Chevron, 467 U.S.] at 842. If, and only if,
      congressional intent is “clear,” that is the end of the inquiry. Ibid. But
      if the court determines that “the statute is silent or ambiguous with
      respect to the specific issue” at hand, the court must, at Chevron’s
      second step, defer to the agency’s interpretation if it “is based on a
      permissible construction of the statute.” Id., at 843.

Loper Bright, 603 U.S. at 379-80.
      The United States Supreme Court in Loper Bright ultimately held that
“Chevron cannot be reconciled with the” federal Administrative Procedures Act,
5 U.S.C. §§ 551-559, “by presuming that statutory ambiguities are implicit
delegations to agencies,” and that Chevron was “fundamentally misguided.” Id. at



                                          7
 399, 407. Therefore, the United States Supreme Court abandoned the doctrine of
Chevron deference. Id. at 412.
      As to the effect of the United States Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright
on our interpretation of Pennsylvania statutes, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court has
explained that, “[p]ursuant to the Supremacy Clause of the United States
Constitution,[6] . . . this Court, like all state courts, is bound by decisions of the
[United States] Supreme Court with respect to the federal Constitution and federal
substantive law.” Commonwealth v. Jemison, 98 A.3d 1254, 1257 (Pa. 2014).
“However, when resolving matters that involve no federal question,” state courts are
“not bound by decisions of the [United States] Supreme Court.” Id.; see also Est. of
Benyo v. Breidenbach, 233 A.3d 774, 783 n.14 (Pa. 2020) (explaining that the
Pennsylvania Supreme Court “has final decision-making authority when interpreting
state statutes”). Furthermore, “[a]s an intermediate appellate court, we must follow
and apply” the decisions of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court “to establish some
measure of predictability and stability in our case law.” Zauflik v. Pennsbury Sch.
Dist., 72 A.3d 773, 783 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2013) (citations and quotation marks omitted),
aff’d, 104 A.3d 1096 (Pa. 2014).
      “Our goal when interpreting a [Pennsylvania] statute is to ascertain and
effectuate the General Assembly’s intent. The plain language of a statute is, as a
general rule, the best indicator of such legislative intent.” Ghaderi v. State Bd. of
Osteopathic Med., 302 A.3d 240, 244 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2023) (citations and quotation
marks omitted). Section 1921 of the Statutory Construction Act of 1972 (Statutory
Construction Act), 1 Pa. C.S. § 1921, sets forth basic statutory construction
principles that guide Pennsylvania courts. That section provides, in relevant part:


      6
          U.S. Const. art. VI, cl. 2.


                                          8
           (a) The object of all interpretation and construction of statutes is to
          ascertain and effectuate the intention of the General Assembly. Every
          statute shall be construed, if possible, to give effect to all its provisions.
          (b) When the words of a statute are clear and free from all ambiguity,
          the letter of it is not to be disregarded under the pretext of pursuing its
          spirit.
          (c) When the words of the statute are not explicit, the intention of the
          General Assembly may be ascertained by considering, among other
          matters:
          ....
              (7) The contemporaneous legislative history.
              (8) Legislative and administrative interpretations of such statute.

1 Pa. C.S. § 1921. Thus, “[w]here the intent of the legislature is clear from the plain
meaning of the statute, courts must not pursue statutory construction. . . . Only when
the language of the statute is ambiguous or not explicit does statutory construction
become necessary.” Twp. of Washington v. Twp. of Upper Burrell, 184 A.3d 1083,
1088 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2018).
          In Povacz II, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, when interpreting Section
2807(f) of the Code7 pertaining to smart meter technology, considered the following

7
    Section 2807(f) of the Code provides, in relevant part:
          (f) Smart meter technology and time of use rates.—
             (1) Within nine months after the effective date of this paragraph, electric
             distribution companies shall file a smart meter technology procurement and
             installation plan with the commission for approval. The plan shall describe the
             smart meter technologies the electric distribution company proposes to install
             in accordance with paragraph (2).
             (2) Electric distribution companies shall furnish smart meter technology as
             follows:
                 (i) Upon request from a customer that agrees to pay the cost of the smart
                 meter at the time of the request.
                 (ii) In new building construction.
                 (iii) In accordance with a depreciation schedule not to exceed 15 years.


                                                   9
 question: “Does Act 129 mandate the system-wide installation of smart meters?”
Povacz II, 280 A.3d at 989. In answering that question, the Court explained that
“Act 129 directed the PUC to ‘adopt an energy efficiency and conservation
[(EE&C)] program to require [EDCs] to adopt and implement cost-effective energy
efficiency and conservation plans to reduce energy demand and consumption’ within
their service territories.” Id. at 992 (quoting 66 Pa. C.S. § 2806.1(a)). The Povacz
II Court then explained that “Section 2806.1 [of the Code] expresses the General
Assembly’s intent to create the EE&C program to include electric customers; hence
the need for a plan based on a fixed existing customer base.” Id. at 993 (emphasis
added); see also id. at 994 (observing that, in order for an EDC to develop a
Procurement and Installation Plan, “an EDC would need to rely on its existing
customer base, not parts of it” (footnote omitted)).
      Based upon the General Assembly’s expressed intent, the Pennsylvania
Supreme Court held:
      Our comprehensive reading of Act 129 leads us to conclude that the
      statute is not ambiguous and that Section 2807(f)(2) [of the Code]
      imposes a mandate on EDCs to furnish smart meter technology to all
      electric customers within an electric distribution service area,
      regardless of a customer’s preference. In reaching this conclusion, we
      have considered Section 2807(f)(2) in its context as the implementation
      provision of Act 129.
      ....
      If, as argued by [the c]ustomers, retail customers could choose the type
      of EE&C measures they prefer, including the type of electric meter,
      then EDCs could not comply with the requirements of the EE&C
      program or their individual PUC-approved plans, and the General
      Assembly’s goal of reducing energy consumption and demand in
      Pennsylvania would not be realized.

Id. at 992-993 (footnote omitted) (emphasis added); see also id. at 998 (“Considering
the overall goal of Act 129 to promote energy efficiency and conservation in


                                         10
 Pennsylvania, the plain language of Section 2807(f)(2) mandates the system-wide
installation of smart meter technology, including smart meters, with no opt-out
provision”).
      Subsequently, this Court has applied Povacz II and held that “[t]he
Commission and this Court are bound by the Supreme Court’s ruling. Because the
Supreme Court has ruled that Section 2807(f)(2) of the Code mandated the system-
wide installation of smart meter technology, the Commission properly interpreted
that Act 129 does not include a smart meter opt-out . . . for customers.” Kline, 352
A.3d at 1094 (footnote omitted).
      Here, the Commission concluded that,
      by establishing that there is no “opt-out” permitting a customer to refuse
      smart meter installation, the Supreme Court’s holding in Povacz II is
      controlling on the question. In the present case, the Complainants’
      Exceptions fail to establish any violation by the utility under Section
      1501 of the Code, [66 Pa. C.S. § 1501,] as a prerequisite to seeking an
      accommodation. To the extent the Complainants’ arguments challenge
      the Supreme Court’s holding in Povacz II, that there is no opt out from
      smart meter implementation, we reject the Complainants’ arguments.
      Povacz II is settled law, and we find no merit in the Complainants’
      argument that Povacz II was wrongly decided.

C.R. at 942a (Commission’s Op. & Order).
      Petitioners’ reliance on Loper Bright is misplaced. As explained above, Loper
Bright applies to federal courts interpreting federal statutes. See Loper Bright, 603
U.S. at 379-80, 385. Therefore, Loper Bright does not apply to Pennsylvania courts
when they are interpreting Pennsylvania statutes. See Est. of Benyo, 233 A.3d at 783
n.14; Jemison, 98 A.3d at 1257.
      At a more fundamental level, however, question Petitioners’ reliance on Loper
Bright because, contrary to Petitioners’ assertions, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court
did not defer to the Commission’s interpretation of Act 129 in Povacz II. Instead,


                                         11
 the Court found that Act 129 was not ambiguous and relied on the plain text of the
statute. See Povacz II, 280 A.3d at 992, 998. Therefore, the Povacz II Court did not
apply Chevron deference when it interpreted Act 129. Compare Loper Bright, 603
U.S. at 379-80 (explaining that Chevron deference was applied when a court
determined that a “statute is silent or ambiguous with respect to the specific issue at
hand” (citation and quotation marks omitted)) with Povacz II, 280 A.3d at 998
(stating that “the plain language of Section 2807(f)(2) mandates the system-wide
installation of smart meter technology, including smart meters, with no opt-out
provision.”).8
       For the reasons set forth above, we reject Petitioners’ claims that Loper Bright
requires this Court to take any course of action other than following the Pennsylvania
Supreme Court’s precedent in Povacz II. See Kline, 352 A.3d at 1094; Zauflik, 72
A.3d at 783.

 C. Whether the Installation of a Smart Meter Violates Article I, Section 8 of
                       the Pennsylvania Constitution
       Petitioners next argue, in the alternative, that if Act 129 contains a mandate to
install smart meters, it violates Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution
because it authorizes a warrantless search through the installation of a smart meter.
Petitioners’ Am. Brief at 64-80. Specifically, Petitioners contend that the data
collected by smart meters at fifteen-minute intervals constitutes a search for the
purposes of Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution. Id. at 70-72.
Petitioners assert that West Penn is a state actor because it possesses government-


       8
          We also note that, because the Povacz II Court’s interpretation of Section 2807 of the
Code is based on the plain language of the statute, it is not ambiguous, and therefore, there is no
need to pursue statutory construction. Twp. of Washington, 184 A.3d at 1088; see also Ghaderi,
302 A.3d at 244 (“The plain language of a statute is, as a general rule, the best indicator of such
legislative intent.”).


                                               12
 like powers, such as the power of eminent domain, the power to enter private
property to install meters, and the power to set rates. Id. at 67-69. Petitioners further
note that the actions of private entities who act pursuant to statutory mandate and
regulatory oversight are state actions. Id. at 68. Petitioners observe that the
“Pennsylvania Supreme Court has recognized that public utilities perform functions
‘imbued with the public interest.’” Id. at 69 (citing purportedly Pa. Pub. Util.
Comm’n v. Israel, 356 A.2d 325, 331 (Pa. 1976)). Further, Petitioners claim that
“[c]onstitutional protections ‘cannot be evaded by the simple expedient of vesting
authority in a private entity.’” Id. (citing purportedly Kremer v. Cox, 114 A.2d 509,
512 (Pa. 1955)). Petitioners maintain that, because Article I, Section 8 of the
Pennsylvania Constitution provides greater protections than the Fourth Amendment
to the United States Constitution, mandatory smart meter installation is an
unreasonable search. Id. at 78-80 (citing, inter alia, Commonwealth v. Edmunds,
586 A.2d 887 (Pa. 1991)).
       The Commission responds that Petitioners have waived their Article I, Section
8 claim, because Petitioners only argued that smart meter installation violated the
Fourth Amendment in the proceedings before the Commission.9 Commission’s
Brief at 22-23. Alternatively, the Commission contends that, even if not waived,
Petitioners are not entitled to relief because West Penn is not a state actor. See id. at
23-24; see also West Penn’s Brief at 29-30.
       Before turning to the merits of Petitioners’ argument, we reject the contention
that Petitioners waived their constitutional challenge by not raising it before the
Commission. While Pennsylvania Rule of Appellate Procedure 1551 limits our

       9
         “The issue of waiver presents a question of law, and, as such, our standard of review is
de novo and our scope of review is plenary.” Trigg v. Child.’s Hosp. of Pittsburgh of UPMC, 229
A.3d 260, 269 (Pa. 2020).


                                               13
 review of quasijudicial orders of a government unit to “[o]nly questions raised before
the government unit,” it excepts from that limitation “[q]uestions involving the
validity of a statute.” Pa.R.A.P. 1551(a); see also Lehman v. Pa. State Police, 839
A.2d 265, 275 (Pa. 2003) (stating that “facial challenges to a statute’s
constitutionality need not be raised before the administrative tribunal to be reviewed
by an appellate court; [constitutional] challenges to a statute’s application, however,
must be raised before the agency or are waived for appellate review”).
      As to whether Section 2708(f) of the Code violates Article I, Section 8 of the
Pennsylvania Constitution, we have explained the protections afforded to Article I,
Section 8 in terms of its federal counterpart, the Fourth Amendment to the United
States Constitution. In Hughes, we wrote:
      The Fourth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution (Fourth Amendment)
      protects “[t]he right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses,
      papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures.” U.S.
      Const. amend. IV. Similarly, [A]rticle I, [S]ection 8 of the
      Pennsylvania Constitution, Pa. Const. art. I, § 8, affords people the
      same security against unreasonable searches and seizures.
      A “search” occurs when “an expectation of privacy that society is
      prepared to consider reasonable is infringed.” United States v.
      Jacobsen, 466 U.S. 109, 113 . . . (1984). . . .
      ....
      Significant to our analysis here, the Fourth Amendment’s protection
      against unlawful searches and seizures applies to “only governmental
      action.” Jacobsen, 466 U.S. at 113 . . . . It follows, therefore, that “the
      proscriptions of the Fourth Amendment and Article I, [Section] 8 [of
      the Pennsylvania Constitution], do not apply to searches and seizures
      conducted by private [actors].” Commonwealth v. Harris, . . . 817 A.2d
      1033, 1047 ([Pa.] 2002). . . .
      Where the action complained of was taken by a private actor, such as a
      privately-owned utility company, we must examine whether the
      conduct itself involves private or state action. Jackson v. Metropolitan
      Edison Co., 419 U.S. 345, 350 . . . (1974). “The mere fact that a
      business is subject to state regulation does not by itself convert its

                                          14
        action into that of the State for purposes of the Fourteenth Amendment.
       Nor does the fact that the regulation is extensive and detailed, as in the
       case of most public utilities, do so.” Id. (footnote and citation omitted).
       “[T]he inquiry must be whether there is a sufficiently close nexus
       between the State and the challenged action of the regulated entity so
       that the action of the latter may be fairly treated as that of the State
       itself.” Jackson, 419 U.S. at 351.
       ....
       Pennsylvania courts have historically “rejected the contention that the
       furnishing of utility services is . . . a state function.” Jackson, 419 U.S.
       at 353 . . . . In Jackson, the U.S. Supreme Court also rejected the
       contention that a utility is a state actor even where the utility is “a
       heavily regulated, privately owned utility, enjoying at least a partial
       monopoly in the providing of electrical service within its territory” and
       takes action “in a manner which the [PUC] found permissible under
       state law.” Id. at 358 . . . .

Hughes, 322 A.3d at 990-91 (some citations omitted).
       This Court in Hughes, based upon the above reasoning, concluded that EDCs
are not state actors with regard to the installation of smart meters. We wrote:
       Although Act 129 mandates [PPL Electric Utilities Corporation (PPL)]
       and other EDCs to install smart meters in their territories, PPL’s
       compliance with Act 129 does not make it an agent of the state. There
       is no evidence in this case that the government controls the operations
       of PPL or that PPL acts as an agent of the government.

Hughes, 322 A.3d at 992. We likewise conclude, here, that Act 129—specifically
Section 2708(f) of the Code—does not violate Article I, Section 8 of the
Pennsylvania Constitution by authorizing a so-called “warrantless search” of data
through the installation of a smart meter because West Penn, like other EDCs, is not
a state actor.10 See id. at 990-92.

       10
         Petitioners’ argument to the contrary is without merit. Petitioners turn to “Pennsylvania
Public Utility Commission v. Israel, 356 A.2d 325 (Pa. 1976),” and “Kremer v. Cox, 114 A.2d 509
(Pa. 1955),” in support of their argument that public utilities are state actors for Fourth Amendment
purposes, but these two cases, as cited, do not appear to exist. There is a case with the name



                                                15
       D. Whether Petitioners’ Procedural Due Process Rights Were Violated
        In their final issue, Petitioners claim that ALJ DeVoe violated their due
process rights by denying their request for an extension of time to file a brief.
Petitioners’ Am. Brief at 81-85. Specifically, Petitioners argue that the denial of
their extension request was unreasonable and the death of a family member
constituted good cause for an extension of the deadline. Id. at 81-82. Petitioners
also claim that if the extension had been granted, they would have discovered the
testimony of former State Representative Thomas Yewcic regarding the General
Assembly’s intent when it enacted Act 129. Id. at 82. Petitioners assert that if ALJ
DeVoe granted their request for an extension of time they could have presented their
argument about how Loper Bright affected Povacz II. Id. at 83. Petitioners conclude
that they were deprived of a meaningful opportunity to present their case, and this
violated their due process rights. Id. at 85; see also Petitioners’ Am. Reply Brief at
28.
        The Commission responds that Petitioners had ample opportunity to review
the transcript between August 9, 2020, and December 5, 2023, because this matter
had been stayed before the Commission until November 9, 2023. Commission’s

“Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission v. Israel” at 52 A.2d 317 (Pa. 1947), but it stands for the
proposition that under the former Public Utility Law of 1937, the Commission was able to institute
proceedings in the Court of Common Pleas of Dauphin County to enjoin the defendants from
operating an uncertified taxicab service. The actual PUC v. Israel case has no bearing on whether
public utilities can be held liable for Fourth Amendment violations as state actors. See Pa. Pub.
Util. Comm’n v. Israel, 52 A.2d at 322-24. Petitioners’ amended brief and amended reply brief
are rife with citations to other cases that do not exist and/or non-existent quotations from actual
cases.
        Based on the foregoing, we have serious questions about the authenticity of the Petitioners’
citations, which begs the question from whence they came, and caution Petitioners not to cite or
otherwise rely on non-existent cases in violation of the Rules of Appellate Procedure. See
Pa.R.A.P. 2119(a) (providing that litigants must cite to “pertinent” legal authorities in their
appellate briefs).


                                                16
 Brief at 26-27; see also West Penn’s Brief at 31 (observing that “Petitioners were
given a series of extensions of time in a complaint proceeding that was initiated six
years prior to the PUC’s final decision”). The Commission claims that the filing of
briefs was optional because ALJ DeVoe had advised the parties that, because she
had reviewed the transcript and exhibits, she was able to render an initial decision
without the aid of briefs. Commission’s Brief at 27 (citing C.R. at 841a). Further,
the Commission argues that Petitioners were not deprived of the opportunity to
present their case, because they fully participated in the hearing and were able to
present their argument in its entirety. Id. at 27-28.
      The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has “recognized that due process principles
apply to quasi-judicial or administrative proceedings, and whether a due process
violation has occurred raises a question of law for which this Court’s standard of
review is de novo and scope of review is plenary.” Pascal v. City of Pittsburgh
Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 259 A.3d 375, 382 (Pa. 2021) (citations omitted and some
formatting altered). “[T]he basic elements of procedural due process [are] adequate
notice, opportunity to be heard, and the chance to defend oneself . . . .” Cresco, Inc.
v. Pa. Pub. Util. Comm’n, 622 A.2d 997, 1000 (Pa. Cmwlth.), appeal denied, 637
A.2d 292 (Pa. 1993). Moreover, “due process is fully applicable to adjudicative
hearings involving substantial property rights. We have recognized that . . . [a]
fundamental requirement of due process is the opportunity to be heard at a
meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.” Id. (citations and quotation marks
omitted) (emphases in original). A party is not denied due process when that party




                                          17
 fails to avail themselves of the process afforded them. See, e.g., Allison v. Pa. Hum.
Rels. Comm’n, 716 A.2d 689, 694 (Pa. Cmwlth. 1998).11
       Lastly, we observe that the Commission “is the ultimate finder of fact in
formal complaint proceedings. As factfinder, the [Commission] is empowered to
review record evidence, make credibility determinations, and accord evidentiary
weight.” Hughes, 322 A.3d at 993-94.
       Based on our review of the record, we disagree with Petitioners’ claim that
ALJ DeVoe’s denial of their motion for extension of time to file a brief deprived
them of an opportunity to be heard. First, Petitioners had the opportunity to be heard
at the evidentiary hearing on February 20, 2020. C.R. at 251a. Second, ALJ
DeVoe’s order stated that the parties may, but were not required to, file briefs. Id.
at 768a. Third, Petitioners did not include a request to reopen the record in their
motion for an extension of time.12 Id. at 771a-72a. Fourth, Petitioners filed
exceptions with the Commission to ALJ DeVoe’s initial decision in which they
raised additional issues such as their claim that Povacz II was wrongly decided and
former Representative Yewcic’s testimony about Act 129. Id. at 865a-72a.

       11
            We note that the petitioners in Allison argued that they had been denied due process
because the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission entered a decision without affording the
petitioners the opportunity to file a post-hearing brief, but this Court explained the petitioners
failed to file a brief and failed to request an extension of time to file a brief. See Allison, 716 A.2d
at 693-94.
       12
           We note that the Commission’s regulations provide that the record is closed at the
conclusion of the hearing and additional matters will not be considered unless the Commission
grants a motion to reopen the record. See 52 Pa. Code §§ 5.431(a)-(b), 5.571(a). Petitioners did
not include a request to reopen the record in the request for an extension of time to file briefs that
they submitted to ALJ DeVoe. Further, after Petitioners filed with the Commission exceptions to
ALJ DeVoe’s initial decision, they did not request that the Commission reopen the record to
consider additional evidence such as former Representative Yewcic’s testimony. As explained
above, a party is not denied due process when that party fails to avail itself of the process afforded
it. See Allison, 716 A.2d at 694.


                                                  18
        For these reasons, we conclude that Petitioners had the opportunity to be heard
at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner in the proceedings before the
Commission, which is the ultimate factfinder, not the ALJ. See Hughes, 322 A.3d
at 993-994. Therefore, the Commission did not violate Petitioners’ due process
rights. See Schmukle, 302 A.3d at 250 n.6; Cresco, 622 A.2d at 1000.
                                    IV. CONCLUSION
       For the reasons set forth above, we affirm the Commission’s order dismissing
Petitioners’ complaint with prejudice.13
